chunks: Blocks of an MCU and an MPU. The question: What are the blocks of a microcontroller and microprocessor?
Inside a microcontroller, a processor core is joined by wires, called a bus, to the memory and to hardware blocks that do specific jobs, such as timers and serial ports.
Support blocks handle the clock, reset, interrupts and bulk data copying.
A microprocessor chip has the processor, a small fast memory called a cache, and controllers that reach outside memory chips. The main memory and storage sit off the chip.
Picture a small office. The manager (the processor core) works at a desk.
A filing cabinet holds procedures (program memory), and a whiteboard holds today's notes (working memory).
A receptionist taps the manager's shoulder when something urgent arrives.
Departments do specialist jobs (the peripherals), and a courier carries parcels between them so the manager doesn't have to.
Hallways connect every room, and the wall clock sets the pace.
Masters (CPU and DMA) reach slaves (flash, SRAM, peripherals) through the bus matrix. Peripherals raise events into the NVIC, which interrupts the CPU.
Clock and reset blocks feed everything.
Core: the part of the chip that runs instructions. Bus: the shared wires that carry addresses and data between blocks.
Peripheral: a hardware block that does one job, such as a timer, a serial port or an analog-to-digital converter ("How an MCU talks to peripherals").
Interrupt: a signal from a block that makes the core pause and handle an event. DMA: a helper block that copies data between memory and peripherals without the core.
Register: a small storage slot that controls a block. Software writes to it like writing to a memory address.
An analog-to-digital converter (a block that turns a voltage into a number) produces 1 million numbers, or samples, per second.
If each sample interrupted the core, and each interrupt cost 100 clock ticks, the core would need 100 million ticks per second.
A 72 megahertz core has only 72 million, an impossible 139% load.
With DMA, the samples are copied into memory automatically, and the core is interrupted only when a whole block of memory (a buffer) is full. That is the whole idea.

"An MCU is a CPU core connected through a bus matrix to on-chip flash and SRAM, plus clock and reset logic, an interrupt controller, DMA, and peripherals: GPIO, timers, serial ports, ADC/DAC, a watchdog and a debug port, all memory-mapped.
A microprocessor has the CPU cores with caches and an MMU, a DRAM controller, an interrupt controller and I/O blocks, but the DRAM, boot storage and power management are separate chips on the board."
